stances.claim: It is ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan -- not 'the ICC' -- that has applied for arrest warrants against Netanyahu et al. and Sinwar et al.; news sources conflating the two are mistaken.

Under the Rome Statute, ICC jurisdiction requires (1) RS-listed crimes, (2) commission in the territory of a member-state or by its national, (3) active state membership, and (4) the absence of complementarity (the state must be 'unwilling or unable to prosecute').

The Panel of Experts Report (May 20, 2024) treating Palestine including Gaza as a State for ICC purposes -- while omitting Israel's non-membership and the complementarity requirement -- is doctrinally incomplete; Israel may be 'willing and able to prosecute,' given its 'functioning prosecutorial offices' and 'active, competent, and independent' judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-completeness audit of the Panel Report

stances.claim: CJ's personal acquaintance with then-future Israeli CJ Dorit Beinisch and his May 2000 visit to the Israeli Supreme Court confirm -- to him -- that the Israeli judiciary has remained 'active, competent, and independent to this day,' which is material to the complementarity question.

CJ does not know enough about Hamas to assess the Panel's allusion to it as 'part of the Palestinian state,' and acknowledges that countries that have designated Hamas a 'terrorist organization' may treat ICC action as 'irrelevant' because they 'can deal with Hamas more effectively.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban clarifies, against news sources that conflated the two, that it is ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan -- not the ICC itself -- that is asking the Pre-Trial Chamber for arrest warrants against Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu et al. and Hamas's Yahya Sinwar et al. for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Initial denunciations came swiftly: Israel ('historical disgrace'); Hamas ('strongly condemn'); Netanyahu rejecting 'with disgust' the comparison between democratic Israel and mass-murdering Hamas; US President Biden ('outrageous... there is no equivalence -- none'); Germany ('false impression of equivalence'). Khan grounds his applications on Israel's 'widespread and systematic attack against the Palestinian civilian population' in Gaza and on Sinwar's 'criminal responsibility' for the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas blitz that included hostage-taking, rape and other sexual violence, and torture. CJ then sets out the Rome Statute architecture: July 17, 1998; 124 member-states (non-members include the US, Russia, China, and Israel); four principal organs (Presidency, Judicial Divisions, Office of the Prosecutor, Registry); and a four-element jurisdictional rule -- RS-listed crimes, committed in a member-state's territory or by its national, while membership is active, and only absent 'complementarity' (the state being 'unwilling or unable to prosecute'). To bridge the membership gap, Khan convened a Panel of Experts in International Law in January 2024; its nine-page Report dated May 20, 2024 concluded that the ICC has jurisdiction and that Palestine including Gaza is a State for ICC purposes -- but CJ flags that the Report 'made no mention of Israel's non-membership' and 'omitted the requirement for complementarity,' even though Israel has 'functioning prosecutorial offices' and a judiciary CJ has personally observed (during his May 2000 visit) to be 'active, competent, and independent.' He recalls inviting Israeli CJ Dorit Beinisch -- then not yet CJ -- to the PH SC's 2001 Centenary Celebrations to speak on 'Protecting Civil Liberties in a State of Continuing Emergency,' and quotes her letter from his book 'Reforming the Judiciary' (pp. 178-179). He admits he does not know enough about Hamas to assess the Panel's allusion to it as 'part of the Palestinian state,' noting that countries that have designated Hamas a terrorist organization may treat ICC action as irrelevant because they can 'deal with Hamas more effectively than the ICC.'
